opus-5.5.text:
Well, I think part of it is that I try to hold my views about timelines with a lot of humility, because the track record of confident predictions in this area isn't great in either direction. People in the 1960s thought human-level AI was a couple of decades away, and they were badly wrong. More recently, many sceptics thought systems would never do the things they're doing now, and they were also badly wrong. So I don't find any particular date astonishing. I find a wide spread of dates quite plausible.

But to be more concrete, there are a few reasons why 2040 or 2045 doesn't strike me as surprising.

The first is that current capabilities are very impressive but also quite uneven. These systems can write fluent essays, pass difficult exams, and solve a lot of coding problems. Yet they still struggle with things like reliably carrying out long, multi-step tasks over days or weeks, noticing and correcting their own mistakes, and operating autonomously in messy real-world settings. It's not obvious how much of that gap closes with more scale, and how much needs conceptual breakthroughs we haven't had yet. If it's the latter, those breakthroughs could come quickly, or they could take a decade or two.

The second concerns compute growth. The recent progress has been driven substantially by scaling up training compute by enormous factors year after year. That trend can't go on forever at the same rate. At some point you hit constraints: the cost of training runs reaching tens or hundreds of billions of dollars, the availability of chips, the energy and data centre capacity needed, and possibly running out of high-quality training data. Extrapolating a curve that's been growing several-fold per year is exactly the sort of thing that tends to look right until it suddenly doesn't. When you scale that fast, even a modest slowdown pushes things out by many years.

Third, there's a question of what returns you're getting from scale. We've seen evidence that some of the gains from simply making pre-training bigger may be diminishing, and that a lot of recent progress has come from other places, like reinforcement learning on reasoning, or spending more compute at inference time. Those are real advances, but some of them are expensive in ways that don't compound as neatly. If you have to spend far more compute to get each additional increment of capability, the road to something like AGI could be longer than a straight-line extrapolation suggests.

And finally, there's the definitional issue. "AGI" means different things to different people. If you mean a system that can do essentially any cognitive task a skilled human can do, including long-horizon autonomous work in the real economy, that's a very high bar. It's possible we get systems that look superhuman in many narrow respects well before we clear that bar in full.

So my view is that short timelines, say within the next five years, are a serious possibility and we should be preparing for them. That's important from a safety perspective, because the cost of being unprepared is so high. But I'd also put substantial probability on things taking until the 2040s or beyond. Both of those can be true at once. What I'd find astonishing is someone being very confident either way.

fable-5.1.text:
Well, I think the first thing to say is that I don't find it astonishing because I don't think the current trajectory can continue in the way that people often assume. A lot of the excitement about very short timelines comes from extrapolating the compute scaling we've seen over the last several years, and that scaling has been extraordinary. Training compute for frontier models has been growing by something like four or five times per year. But if you actually ask where that growth has come from, most of it hasn't been from chips getting better at the rate Moore's law would predict. It's come from spending vastly more money on each training run — and from a larger fraction of the world's chip production being devoted to AI.

And those are things that can't keep going indefinitely. If you're spending a hundred million dollars on a training run and growing that by four times a year, pretty soon you're talking about tens of billions, then hundreds of billions, and then you're talking about a meaningful fraction of global GDP. At some point you hit a wall, not because of any deep technical limit, but simply because the economy isn't big enough to sustain that rate of increase. I think we're actually quite close to that point. So the question becomes: what happens to progress when the compute growth slows back down to something closer to the underlying rate of hardware improvement, which is more like a doubling every couple of years rather than every few months?

My guess is that progress doesn't stop, but it does slow substantially. The last few years have been a kind of catch-up phase, where we're harvesting an overhang of possibilities that we didn't previously have the resources to try. Once you've used up that overhang, you're back to a slower, more ordinary pace of scientific advance. And if that's right, then timelines of 2040 or 2045 start to look fairly natural rather than surprising.

There's also the point that there are still things these systems can't do that seem quite important for anything we'd want to call AGI. They don't learn continually from experience the way a person does. They struggle with long, multi-step tasks where errors compound. They're inconsistent in ways that are hard to iron out. I'm not saying these are unsolvable — I'd be quite surprised if they were — but I don't think we should assume they fall out of another year or two of scaling. Some of them might require genuinely new ideas, and new ideas arrive on their own schedule.

So I hold a reasonably wide distribution. I wouldn't be shocked if things went much faster than I expect — that's part of why I take the risks seriously. But I also think the people who say 2027 or 2028 are putting an enormous amount of weight on a trend that is, for structural economic reasons, about to bend. And I think that's worth saying clearly, because it matters a great deal for how we prepare.

astra-6.text:
Well, I think there’s a big difference between saying that AGI could arrive very soon and saying that it would be astonishing if it took another fifteen or twenty years. I take the first possibility seriously, but I don’t think we know enough to rule out the second.

The compute projections are one part of the argument. Even if we knew exactly how much compute would be available in 2040, we’d still need to know what capabilities that would buy us. We can observe how systems improve as we scale them, but translating that into a date at which they can do essentially all the cognitive work humans can do is a further step. That’s where a lot of the uncertainty lies.

It could turn out that the current approach, with fairly straightforward improvements, gets us there. Or there could be important things missing that require further breakthroughs. The remarkable progress we’ve seen is evidence for the first possibility, but it doesn’t establish it.

So I’d want to keep a broad range of dates in mind. And that isn’t a reason to be complacent: a substantial chance of AGI arriving soon is enough to make preparation urgent. You don’t need to be certain about a short timeline to take it very seriously.

sol-6.1.text:
Well, I think there’s a difference between thinking that something could happen quite soon and being astonished if it took another fifteen or twenty years. I’m very open to the possibility that AGI comes sooner than that. But we don’t yet know how much more is needed, or whether the things that are missing will yield to the same methods that have produced the progress we’ve seen so far.

The compute projections are impressive, but compute isn’t itself a measure of how close we are to AGI. To get from one to the other, you need assumptions about how improvements in performance translate into increasingly general capabilities, and about whether that relationship will continue. Those assumptions might be right, but I wouldn’t want to be overwhelmingly confident in them.

So I’d put substantial weight on short timelines, while still leaving substantial weight on it taking longer. What would surprise me is if we already had enough evidence to narrow the date down very tightly.
